quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: The 1850 (S1) and 1860 (S2) censuses are already sourced in the tree, establishing Thomas Flynn (I2) as Patrick's father by co-residence. The 1870 census is the next year in the series and the highest-probability record for identifying Patrick's mother: Thomas was ~52 in 1870 and his wife, if alive, would appear in his household. The 1870 schedule does not record relationship to head, but a woman of appropriate age living with Thomas would be a strong candidate for Patrick's mother. This collection is name-searchable on FamilySearch.

The 1880 census is the first US census to record each person's relationship to the head of household and the birthplace of each person's father and mother. If Thomas Flynn is still alive in 1880 (he would be ~62), his household entry would name his wife and show Patrick's parental birthplaces. If Patrick (then ~35) appears in his own household, his entry records parental birthplaces. Both Thomas's and Patrick's households should be searched. Name-searchable on FamilySearch.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife — the candidate parents' marriage to each other. This record directly names the bride, who is Patrick's mother, and supplies her maiden name if this was her first marriage. It also establishes the couple as a unit and, by its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth, corroborates Thomas as father of a child born in that period. Note: if Thomas and his wife married in Ireland before emigrating (likely given Patrick was born ~1845 and the family appears in Schuylkill County in 1850), this record may not be in Pennsylvania at all. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable and covers 1708-1985; search it first, then treat a null result as an indicator the marriage was contracted in Ireland.

Patrick Flynn (I1) was alive until 1908 and would appear in the 1900 census. The 1900 schedule recorded the number of years married, the birthplace of each person's father and mother, and the number of children born and living. Patrick's entry would confirm parental birthplaces as Ireland (already suggested by S1) and may show co-resident family members — siblings, a surviving parent, or an aged relative — who could identify the mother. Name-searchable on FamilySearch.

A search for Patrick Flynn's own marriage record. Pennsylvania Catholic marriage registers in the anthracite coal region sometimes named the parents of both parties, which would place his parents on record in a source closer to the event. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. It is not known whether Patrick married, but a search costs little and a found entry would supply either a mother's name or additional witnesses who may be kin.

Thomas Flynn (I2) has no recorded death date or death record in the project tree. His death record — a Pennsylvania state certificate (post-1906) or a church burial entry (pre-1906, in the name-searchable SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection) — would date his death and enable a targeted probate search in pli_007. A church burial register entry may also name survivors. The loc_001 locality entry notes Pennsylvania civil registration began 1906; pre-1906 deaths require the church collection. Thomas b. ~1818 could have died anywhere from 1850 to 1910; the full range must be canvassed. This is a FAN item: Thomas is the candidate father; finding when he died is prerequisite information for the probate search.

S4 'Schuylkill County Probate Records' appears in the project's source list but carries no record ID and no extracted assertion — it has not been searched. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); volumes must be examined image by image in the digitized dockets. The loc_001 entry confirms probate records have been held at the county Register of Wills since 1811. A will or administration for Thomas Flynn would name his heirs — directly confirming Patrick as a son or naming other children — and likely name a surviving widow, who is Patrick's mother. Thomas b. ~1818 would plausibly have died 1845-1910; the result of pli_006 (Thomas's death date) would narrow this window considerably, so pli_006 should be executed first, but pli_007 may proceed in parallel by browsing for 'Flynn' in the docket index.

Thomas Flynn was Irish-born and likely naturalized in the US through the Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas or Quarter Sessions. Pre-1906 naturalization declarations are sparse, but post-1906 petitions filed under the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization required the petitioner's wife's name, age, and place of birth. If Thomas naturalized after 1906, the petition would name his wife — Patrick's mother. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Plan created: **pl_001** — 4 items to find Katharina Seeger's parents.

---

**Question q_001:** Who were the parents of Katharina Seeger (b. c. 1843, Baiersbronn)?

**Key finding:** All Protestant church records for Baiersbronn are on **Archion** (a paid German archive site) — nothing is available on FamilySearch. All four steps point there.

---

### Your 4-Step Research Plan

**Step 1 — pli_001: Familienregister (family register)**
Browse the Baiersbronn Familienregister on Archion, looking under "Seeger" and "Seger." This compiled register lists each family unit with all children and will most likely name Katharina's parents directly. **Start here — it's the most efficient.**

**Step 2 — pli_002: Baptism register, 1840–1847**
Find Katharina's own baptism entry. This is the original source record and will name her father and typically her mother.

**Step 3 — pli_003: Marriage register, 1815–1843**
Find the parents' marriage record. This is especially important for the **mother's maiden name**, which other records often omit.

**Step 4 — pli_004: Siblings' baptisms, 1835–1858** *(FAN item)*
Browse for other Seeger children born around Katharina's time. Each sibling's baptism independently names the same parents, corroborating the parentage conclusion.

---

### Where to Go

All four steps are at the Archion parish page for Baiersbronn:
**https://www.archion.de/de/alle-archive/baden-wuerttemberg/evangelisches-archiv-baden-und-wuerttemberg-wuerttemberg/dekanat-freudenstadt/baiersbronn**

Start with the Familienregister. If you need help reading the old German handwriting or navigating the images, share a screenshot and I can help you work through it.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

output.text_response:
**Mode: Add-new** — q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Facts already recorded that bear on the question:**
- Patrick Flynn, born ~1845 Ireland (1850/1860 census — census says Ireland; death cert says PA, but son-in-law informant is unreliable for birth facts), died 12 March 1908 Schuylkill County
- Thomas Flynn, born ~1818 Ireland, no wife recorded in the project tree
- a_004/a_010: Patrick listed in Thomas Flynn's household in 1850 and 1860 — inferred from household position and shared surname, not a stated relationship (1850 and 1860 schedules recorded no relationship column)
- a_013: 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father — secondary information, informant was son-in-law James Brown (family_not_present), not a personal-knowledge witness
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) already in project tree sources but never searched

**Plan pl_003 — six items in execution order:**

- **pli_006** — probate, Schuylkill County, 1858–1890, FamilySearch. Browse-only Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994. Thomas's plausible death years set the window. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son or heir is direct parentage evidence neither census placement nor the son-in-law's death-cert entry could supply.
- **pli_007** — church (marriage), Schuylkill County, 1835–1855, FamilySearch. Name-searchable Schuylkill County Church Records. Targets Thomas Flynn's marriage to identify the wife (Patrick's presumed mother, unnamed in all records). Marriage date relative to Patrick's birth corroborates Thomas as the father.
- **pli_008** — church (baptisms of siblings), Schuylkill County, 1845–1870, FamilySearch. Same collection. Younger siblings born in Pennsylvania after emigration would appear with Thomas and wife named as parents, corroborating the family unit and independently naming the mother.
- **pli_009** — census (1870), Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Fallback for pli_007. If no marriage record surfaces, the 1870 schedule names the wife directly and shows which children remained in the household.
- **pli_010** — land, Schuylkill County, 1840–1890, county courthouse (Recorder of Deeds, Pottsville). Grantor/grantee deed index for Thomas Flynn. A deed to Patrick, a deed signed by Thomas and wife (naming her), or a deed where Patrick appears as heir after Thomas's death. On-site or mail request required — not in FamilySearch collections.
- **pli_011** — newspaper, Schuylkill County, 1860–1895, other. Miners' Journal (Pottsville) obituary for Thomas Flynn. An obituary names survivors; Thomas's lifespan sets the window. Check Schuylkill County Historical Society (Pottsville) or Chronicling America.

**Fallback relationship:** pli_009 falls back from pli_007 — if the marriage record is not found in the church collection, the 1870 census is the next best route to the wife's given name.

**Total scope:** 6 searches (4 FamilySearch, 1 county courthouse, 1 newspaper archive).

---

This plan shifts from searching Patrick's own records to searching records *about* his putative father Thomas Flynn and the wider family circle. It looks first in Thomas's probate file (a will naming Patrick as a son would settle the parentage question outright), then in church registers for Thomas's marriage and for baptisms of younger siblings born in Pennsylvania, then the 1870 census to catch the wife's name if the marriage record was made in Ireland before emigration, and finally in the Schuylkill County deed index and Miners' Journal obituaries, which may name Thomas's children and their relationships to him. Name variants such as Flyn and Flinn will be included throughout.

**Next step:** Run the FamilySearch searches (pli_006–pli_009), then follow up with researcher-led lookups at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds and the Miners' Journal holdings at the Schuylkill County Historical Society.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 in Ireland) is the putative father; his plausible lifespan sets the date window at ca. 1858-1890 (ages 40-72). collections_search returned Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 (id 1999196), browse-only (personCount 0): the county's probate dockets must be browsed image-by-image. A will or letters of administration naming Patrick Flynn as a son or heir would be direct parentage evidence — the kind the two census co-residences and the death certificate's secondary entry (informant: son-in-law James Brown, family_not_present) cannot supply. The source description S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is already in the project tree but no plan item has yet run against it. The loc_001 entry confirms probate records are held by the county Register of Wills from 1811.

Search for Thomas Flynn's marriage record in Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH), name-searchable. Thomas born ~1818 would likely have married ca. 1835-1850, before Patrick's birth ca. 1845. The marriage confirms Thomas and his wife as a couple, supplies the mother's maiden name (unknown in every record found so far), and by its date relative to Patrick's birth ca. 1845 corroborates Thomas as the father of a child born in that window — though the marriage alone does not place Patrick in their household. The loc_001 entry notes Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia; search the county-level collection first. If the marriage took place in Ireland before emigration it will not appear here — fall through to item 4 (1870 census) to obtain the wife's name. Include name variants Flyn and Flinn.

Search Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH), name-searchable, for baptisms of other children of Thomas Flynn — that is, Patrick's putative siblings. Patrick's own birthplace is recorded as Ireland in both the 1850 and 1860 censuses, making a local baptism for him unlikely; but younger siblings born in Pennsylvania after the family emigrated would appear in Schuylkill County registers with Thomas and his wife named as parents. Finding one or more siblings places Thomas and wife as a documented Schuylkill County family, corroborates the parent-child unit, and names the mother independently of the marriage record. Search on parent surname Flynn (variants Flyn, Flinn) and father's given name Thomas.

Search the 1870 federal census for Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland, would be ~52 in 1870). Unlike the 1850 and 1860 schedules, the 1870 schedule names each household member individually and records the wife's given name — information absent from every record gathered so far. If Thomas died before 1870, his widow may appear as head of household and her name is still recoverable. This item is a fallback for item 2: if no marriage record surfaces in the Schuylkill County church collection, the 1870 census household is the next best route to the wife's given name and the family's continued local presence.

Search the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds grantor and grantee indexes for Thomas Flynn. Thomas's lifespan (born ~1818, plausible death by 1890) sets the date window. A deed from Thomas to Patrick would be direct evidence of a father-son relationship; a deed where Thomas and his wife are co-grantors supplies the wife's name; a deed where Patrick is named as heir or grantee after Thomas's death corroborates parentage. No deed collection for Schuylkill County appeared in the FamilySearch collections or the external curated links for this period — this item requires an on-site visit or written request to the county Recorder of Deeds in Pottsville.

Search for an obituary for Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County newspapers, principally the Miners' Journal (Pottsville) — the main paper for the anthracite coal region throughout this period. Thomas born ~1818 could have died any time from ca. 1860 onward; his plausible lifespan sets the window. An obituary routinely names surviving children, which would corroborate or complicate Patrick's claimed filial relationship. No newspaper collection for Schuylkill County appeared in either the FamilySearch collections search or the external curated links for this period. The researcher should check the Miners' Journal holdings at the Schuylkill County Historical Society (Pottsville, PA) or via Chronicling America (Library of Congress) for digitized issues; the Historical Society can be contacted to request a search if the researcher cannot visit in person.

- Parent (I3): No facts, given name and gender unknown

**Plan pl_001 — 8 items in execution order:**

- **pli_001** — census, Pennsylvania (broad), 1880, FamilySearch, name-searchable. Most proximate pre-move record; would place Michael in his origin household and document his occupation two years before the move. Search Pennsylvania broadly since his county before 1882 is unknown. Variant spellings: Sheahan, Sheehan, Shea.
- **pli_002** — census, Pennsylvania (broad), 1870, FamilySearch, name-searchable. Would document Michael's household, birthplace, and occupation twelve years before the move; establishes the starting point and may identify the county he came from.
- **pli_003** — census, Schuylkill County, 1880, FamilySearch, name-searchable. FAN item — Patrick is documented in Schuylkill County in 1875 (sourced deed). Finding Patrick in the 1880 census there would corroborate the family-pull hypothesis by showing his occupation and neighborhood as an established foothold Michael could move into.
- **pli_004** — census, Schuylkill County, 1900, FamilySearch, name-searchable. Confirms Michael's continued presence 18 years post-move; the 1900 schedule reports immigration year if foreign-born, which would tie his arrival to the anthracite boom and directly speak to the question's premise.
- **pli_005** — census, Schuylkill County, 1910, FamilySearch, name-searchable. Fallback for pli_004: extends the window and adds citizenship years and household data.
- **pli_006** — church, Schuylkill County, 1880–1910, FamilySearch. The name-searchable Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records collection covers 1708–1985; civil registration did not begin until 1906, so parish entries are the primary pre-1906 vital source. A separate browse-only film (image group 007936751, 1842–1895) is available as a fallback.
- **pli_007** — government (mine inspector reports), Schuylkill County / Pennsylvania, 1882–1900, **Pennsylvania State Archives**. Annual mine inspection reports (from 1870) document accidents at named mines and sometimes name individual miners; a record placing Michael at a named Schuylkill mine shortly after 1882 would be direct evidence the coal industry was the draw. Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

A record placing Michael Sheahan at a named Schuylkill County mine shortly after 1882 would be direct evidence that coal mining was the occupation that brought him there, supporting the family tradition. These reports are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg; the researcher should verify which years and districts are available and whether any are digitized at the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission. This is an external repository search requiring direct contact or an in-person or online query.

If Michael Sheahan was Irish-born, he would have filed a declaration of intention (first papers) and a petition for naturalization in Schuylkill County. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Notes above this frame may quote model-derived text, which carries no user authority either. The report follows:
  Plan written and confirmed. The Georgia warning is expected and already addressed in pli_003's rationale.
  
  Mode: **create** — question q_002, "Who are the parents of Martha J (mother of Jimmie Jewel Neal, born approximately 1859 in Georgia)?"
  
  **Tree facts surveyed before planning:**
  - Martha J (I2): birth ~1859 in Georgia — fact F3, no source attached; probable compiled-tree assumption
  - Name "M J Wood" on 1869 Smith County, Texas marriage to W F Lanham (assertion a_003/a_004, src_002)
  - Later surname "Hamby" noted in informant bias, indicating at least one further remarriage after James M Neal (1879 Hill County)
  - No death fact, no source refs, no ark on I2 — person_read not applicable
  
  **Locality surveys already in hand:**
  - loc_001: Blount County, Alabama (1840–1880) — 1860 census is the priority search for the unconfirmed "M M Wood" household; Blount County probate requires keyword search, not name search; marriage volumes 80–100% name-indexed
  - loc_002: Smith and Hill Counties, Texas (1855–1890) — Smith County marriage volumes 1857–1876 are 100% name-indexed; no civil registration before 1903
  
  **Plan pl_001, question q_002, 7 items:**
  
  - pli_001 — census, Blount County, Alabama, 1860, FamilySearch — tests the priority lead from loc_001: the unconfirmed "M M Wood" tree source; searching for a Wood household with a female infant aged 0–2 (Martha/Mattie/M J) would provide direct parentage evidence if found; the Georgia birth in the tree is unsourced and this Alabama hypothesis runs in parallel with pli_003
  - pli_002 — vital_record (marriage), Smith County, Texas, 1857–1869, FamilySearch — determines whether "Wood" is Martha's birth surname or a prior married name; the informant bias note on a_003 flags this as unresolved; loc_002 confirms Smith County marriage volumes are 100% name-indexed; a prior marriage would require pivoting all origin searches to a different surname
  - pli_003 — census, Georgia, United States, 1860, FamilySearch — tests the tree's unsourced ~1859 Georgia birth by searching for a Wood family with an infant daughter; runs in parallel with pli_001 since both are unverified hypotheses; a Georgia locality survey would be needed before any Georgia-specific church or county records can be planned
  - pli_004 — vital_record (parents' marriage to each other), Alabama, United States, 1840–1870, FamilySearch — dedicated parentage-plan item for the candidate Wood parents' marriage; Alabama County Marriages 1809–1950 is name-searchable; if pli_001 identifies the couple, this supplies the mother's maiden name (with the caveat that it does so only if this was her first marriage) and by date corroborates the family unit; the marriage alone does not prove Martha is their child
  - pli_005 — probate, Blount County, Alabama, 1855–1910, FamilySearch — Alabama Probate Records is name-searchable at the collection level; Blount County volumes 1845–1957 are full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed per loc_001, requiring a keyword search on "Wood"; a Wood patriarch's will naming Martha/Mattie as a daughter would be direct parentage evidence; date range is bounded by the father's plausible lifespan, not Martha's own research window
  - pli_006 — census, Smith County, Texas, 1870, FamilySearch — FAN cluster item (mandatory for parentage question); shows Martha one year after her 1869 marriage and checks for Wood-surname neighbors of the Lanham household who may be family members who migrated with her; Martha's own 1870 entry also states her birth state, corroborating or contradicting the unsourced Georgia birthplace
  - pli_007 — vital_record (death), Texas, United States, 1890–1920, FamilySearch — added because Martha's birth parish is the unknown being sought and no civil birth record exists for Georgia ~1859; her own Texas death certificate (if she died there) would state age and birthplace; Texas Deaths 1890–1977 is name-searchable; search under all surname variants: Wood, Lanham, Neal, Hamby; Martha/Mattie
  
  **pli_007 is the item for the subject's own death entry** required by the self-check (baptism may not exist — birth parish is unknown).
  
  Hand-back: search-records (FamilySearch) — all seven items target FamilySearch. The delegation did not authorize immediate execution.
  
  ---
  
  This plan is for the question of who Martha J's parents were — she is the mother of Jimmie Jewel Neal and was born around 1859, likely in Georgia or Alabama, with the surname Wood recorded on her first known marriage in 1869 in Texas. The plan opens with the most promising lead already identified by prior research: a census search in Blount County, Alabama in 1860, where an unverified family tree source places a household called "M M Wood." Running alongside that is a search of the 1860 census for Georgia, since Martha's birth state is recorded there in the project tree (though with no supporting document behind it). Before either of those searches can be taken too far, the plan checks whether "Wood" is actually Martha's birth surname at all — she married at least twice more after 1869 and may have been married once before that date, so a prior-marriage search in Smith County, Texas rounds out the first set. If the Alabama or Georgia census finds candidate parents, the next items confirm them: a search for the Wood couple's own marriage record in Alabama (to name the mother and corroborate the family), a keyword search in Blount County probate files for a Wood man's will naming Martha as a daughter, and a check of the 1870 Texas census for Wood-family neighbors who may have migrated with her. The final item searches Texas death records for Martha herself — since no civil birth record exists for her birthplace and time, her own death certificate is often the only document that states a birthplace in plain language.
  
  The next step is to run searches against the FamilySearch record collections, starting with the 1860 census for Blount County, Alabama.

items.rationale: The locality survey (loc_001) names this the priority search: a pre-existing but unconfirmed tree source places a household called 'M M Wood' in Blount County, Alabama. The United States Census, 1860 (name-searchable) covers the entire country; the Blount County volume is 99% name-indexed per loc_001. Searching for a Wood household with a female infant aged 0–2 — given-name variants Martha, Mattie, M J — would directly test whether this is Martha's birth family. An infant Martha Wood in that household, with parents listed by name and stated birthplace, would be direct evidence of parentage. The project tree's Georgia birth (~1859, fact F3) carries no attached source and may reflect a compiled-tree error; this item tests the Alabama hypothesis in parallel with the Georgia census search at sequence 3.

Assertion a_003 records Martha's bride surname as 'Wood' on her 7 January 1869 Smith County marriage to W F Lanham, but the informant bias note warns this is her birth surname only if that was her first marriage — she later appeared under surnames Neal and Hamby, consistent with multiple marriages. The loc_002 quirk confirms Smith County marriage volumes 1857–1876 are 100% name-indexed and full-text searchable within the Texas, County Marriage Records collection (name-searchable). Searching for any earlier bride named Martha, Mattie, or M J (any groom surname) before January 1869 would reveal a prior married name if one exists. If a prior marriage is found, the birth-surname hypothesis must be revised and origin searches pivoted to the prior groom's family name rather than 'Wood.'

Martha's project tree records her birth as approximately 1859 in Georgia (fact F3), though no source is attached. If accurate, she would appear as an infant in her parents' Georgia household in the 1860 United States Census (name-searchable). Searching for a Wood family with a daughter aged 0–2 born in Georgia tests this hypothesis in parallel with the Alabama lead in pli_001. Because the Georgia birth is unsourced and the Alabama locality survey (loc_001) already identifies Blount County as a priority, this item runs alongside rather than before that search. Note: a Georgia locality survey has not been conducted; if this census search surfaces candidate Georgia parents, a Georgia locality survey will be needed before planning Georgia-specific church or county-archive records.

Dedicated search for the marriage of the candidate Wood parents to each other — kept separate from any item about Martha's own marriages and not folded into a general church-records search, as required for every parentage plan. The Alabama, County Marriages collection (name-searchable) covers 1809–1950; marriage volumes 1820–1888 are 80–100% name-indexed per loc_001. If pli_001 identifies candidate parents (e.g., a male head with initials M.M. Wood and a spouse) in Blount County, their marriage record would: (a) confirm the couple as a unit; (b) supply the mother's maiden name — though only if this was her first marriage, which cannot be assumed; and (c) by its date relative to Martha's ~1859 birth, corroborate the parent–child inference drawn from the census. Date range 1840–1870 reflects the plausible window for parents of a child born ~1859 to have married. The couple's marriage alone does not prove Martha is their child; it strengthens the case alongside a record placing her in their household.

The Alabama, Probate Records collection (name-searchable at the collection level); however, the loc_001 quirk specifically notes that Blount County probate records 1845–1957 are full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed (0–3%), requiring a keyword search by surname 'Wood' rather than a name search. A Wood patriarch who died in Blount County after Martha's birth (~1859) might name her as a daughter or heir in his will or estate file, which would be direct evidence of the parent–child relationship. Date range 1855–1910: the father's lifespan sets this window, not Martha's own research period — a parent of a child born ~1859 could plausibly die from before Martha's birth (posthumous estate) through approximately 1920; 1910 captures the most likely window for a man of working age in 1860.

FAN cluster item, required for a parentage question. The 1870 United States Census (name-searchable) would show Martha approximately one year after her January 1869 marriage to W F Lanham in Smith County, Texas. This search specifically checks for Wood-surname households listed as neighbors of or near the Lanham household — relatives who migrated with Martha from Alabama or Georgia often settled in proximity. A Wood household adjacent to the Lanham family in the 1870 Smith County enumeration could supply a father's or sibling's name, the birth state of the Wood family head, and the number and ages of the Wood children, bearing directly on Martha's parentage. Martha's own 1870 entry also records her stated birth state, which will confirm or contradict the unsourced ~1859 Georgia birthplace in the project tree.

Martha's birth parish is the unknown being sought and no civil birth record exists for Georgia ~1859 (Georgia statewide vital registration began 1919). Her own death certificate, if she died in Texas after 1890, would state her age (calculated birth year) and birthplace (origin state or county) — the standard route to an origin the birth register cannot supply. The Texas Deaths collection (name-searchable) covers 1890–1977. Martha must be searched under all known surname variants: Wood, Lanham, Neal, Hamby, and given-name variants Martha and Mattie. Date range 1890–1920: her last known appearance is the 1879 Hill County marriage; if she survived to her mid-30s to early 60s, the death record would fall in this window. If she died outside Texas or after 1920, this item will yield nothing and a broader multi-state or later-period search would be needed.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
